options.text: Acute profound hypokalemic metabolic shifts impairing peripheral motor axon action potential conduction across limbs
Transient generalized paroxysmal epileptic seizure discharges originating bilaterally from mesial temporal lobe structures
Emotional activation of the amygdala drives aberrant daytime recruitment of the brainstem REM sleep muscle atonia circuit
Sudden autoimmune autoantibody binding to neuromuscular junction nicotinic receptors inducing flaccid muscle weakness
Acute bilateral ischemic stroke involving corticospinal tract axons traversing the posterior limbs of internal capsules

explanation: Cataplexy represents the intrusion of REM sleep muscle atonia into awake consciousness. Under normal conditions, orexinergic projections from the lateral hypothalamus stabilize brainstem motor circuits against emotional disinhibition. In narcoleptic patients who lack orexin, strong emotions (processed in the limbic system, particularly the amygdala and medial prefrontal cortex) send aberrant excitatory projections to the sublaterodorsal (SLD) nucleus in the pons. The SLD immediately activates glycinergic and GABAergic inhibitory interneurons in the ventromedial medulla, hyperpolarizing spinal alpha motor neurons and producing sudden, flaccid skeletal muscle paralysis identical to normal REM sleep atonia, while cortical consciousness remains fully intact.
high_yield_pearl: Cataplexy mechanism: Emotional limbic (amygdala) stimulation triggers REM-sleep muscle atonia (SLD glycinergic pathway) during wakefulness due to lack of orexin.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 5 & Case 2, 6: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD)
question: A 68-year-old retired naval officer is brought to the sleep clinic by his wife because of violent nighttime behavior. For the past two years, he thrashs, shouts obscenities, punches the air, and kicks violently in his sleep. Last week, he leaped out of bed and tackled a dresser, believing in his dream that he was defending himself against hostile intruders. When awakened, he is instantly alert and vividly recounts the combative dream. Polysomnography during REM sleep shows prominent, sustained skeletal muscle tone on the submental EMG. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Sleep terror disorder (night terrors) occurring during Stage N3 Non-REM slow-wave sleep
Confusional arousals resulting from severe sleep deprivation and obstructive sleep apnea
Nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy causing hypermotor seizures during wake-sleep transitions
Dissociative fugue state triggered by underlying post-traumatic stress disorder
REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) caused by degeneration of brainstem pathways that mediate REM muscle atonia

explanation: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia characterized by the loss of normal skeletal muscle atonia (paralysis) during REM sleep, allowing patients to physically 'act out' their dreams (often vivid, unpleasant, action-filled, or violent dreams involving being attacked or pursued). Patients exhibit complex motor behaviors: punching, flailing, kicking, shouting, and leaping from bed, frequently causing significant traumatic injury to themselves or their bed partner. Unlike Non-REM sleep terrors, when awakened from RBD, the patient is immediately alert, coherent, oriented, and can vividly recall the dream scenario.
high_yield_pearl: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD): Loss of REM atonia $\rightarrow$ patients act out violent dreams. Immediately alert when woken with vivid dream recall.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 5 & Case 6: RBD & Alpha-Synucleinopathies
question: A 70-year-old man diagnosed with REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is counseled regarding the long-term prognosis of his condition. The physician explains that RBD is a powerful, highly specific prodromal marker for a particular category of neurodegenerative diseases. Which group of disorders is this patient at exceptionally high risk of developing over the next 10 to 15 years, and what is the first-line medication for symptom management?

options.text: Prion protein diseases (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and Kuru); managed with high-dose intravenous amantadine
Trinucleotide repeat expansion disorders (Huntington disease and spinocerebellar ataxias); managed with tetrabenazine
Tauopathies (Alzheimer disease and Frontotemporal lobar degeneration); managed with donepezil
Alpha-synucleinopathies (Parkinson disease, Dementia with Lewy Bodies, Multiple System Atrophy); managed with low-dose clonazepam or melatonin
Motor neuron diseases (Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and spinal muscular atrophy); managed with riluzole

explanation: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD) is the strongest known clinical prodromal marker for the $\alpha$-synucleinopathies: Parkinson's Disease (PD), Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB), and Multiple System Atrophy (MSA). Longitudinal studies demonstrate that over 80% of patients with idiopathic RBD eventually phenoconvert to an overt $\alpha$-synuclein neurodegenerative disorder within 10 to 15 years. The underlying pathology is early Lewy body / $\alpha$-synuclein deposition in the lower brainstem tegmentum (specifically the sublaterodorsal nucleus and pedunculopontine area) prior to nigrostriatal or cortical involvement. First-line pharmacotherapy for RBD is bedtime low-dose clonazepam (a long-acting benzodiazepine) or high-dose melatonin, along with environmental bedroom safety modifications.
high_yield_pearl: RBD is a prodromal marker for $\alpha$-synucleinopathies (Parkinson's, Lewy Body Dementia, MSA) in >80% of cases. Treat: Clonazepam or Melatonin + bedroom safety.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 5 & Case 3, 5: Sleep Terrors vs. Nightmares
question: A 6-year-old boy is brought by his parents because of terrifying nighttime episodes. Approximately 90 minutes after falling asleep, he abruptly sits bolt upright in bed screaming incoherently, with wide eyes, sweating, dilated pupils, and a heart rate of 140 bpm. His parents are unable to comfort or awaken him. After 10 minutes, he lies back down and falls asleep. The next morning, he has complete amnesia for the episode. In contrast, an 8-year-old girl wakes up at 5:00 AM crying from a scary dream about a monster, runs to her parents' bedroom, is fully alert, and vividly describes the dream. Which sleep stages do these two conditions represent?

options.text: Sleep terrors occur during relaxed wakefulness; nightmares occur during Stage N2 Non-REM sleep
Sleep terrors occur during active REM sleep; nightmares occur during Stage N2 sleep spindles
Both conditions occur exclusively during Stage N3 sleep but represent different degrees of emotional maturity
Sleep terrors occur during Stage N3 Non-REM slow-wave sleep; nightmares occur during Stage REM sleep
Sleep terrors occur during Stage REM sleep; nightmares occur during Stage N1 Non-REM sleep

explanation: Sleep Terrors (Night Terrors) and Nightmares are classic pediatric parasomnias distinguished by sleep stage and clinical features: 1) Sleep Terrors: Non-REM parasomnia occurring during Stage N3 Slow-Wave Sleep, typically during the first third of the night. Features: abrupt awakening with a piercing scream, intense autonomic arousal (tachycardia, diaphoresis, tachypnea, mydriasis), child is inconsolable and unresponsive to comforting, and has COMPLETE AMNESIA for the event upon waking in the morning. Reassurance is primary. 2) Nightmare Disorder: REM parasomnia occurring during Stage REM sleep, typically in the second half or last third of the night. Features: vivid, frightening dream content; upon waking, the child is immediately fully alert, oriented, easily consoled, and VIVIDLY RECALLS the dream.
high_yield_pearl: Sleep Terrors = Stage N3 Non-REM (first 1/3 of night, scream, autonomic arousal, inconsolable, AMNESIA). Nightmares = Stage REM (late night, alert, REMEMBERS dream).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 5 & Case 5: Sleepwalking (Somnambulism)
question: A 10-year-old boy is found by his parents walking downstairs in the middle of the night 2 hours after bedtime. His eyes are open with a glassy, blank stare. When spoken to, he mumbles unintelligibly, walks into the kitchen, opens the refrigerator, and then allows himself to be guided back to bed without waking up. The next morning, he has no recollection of the event. During which sleep stage did this episode originate, and what is the primary management recommendation?

options.text: Stage N3 Non-REM slow-wave sleep; managed primarily with environmental safety precautions and avoiding sleep deprivation
Stage REM sleep; managed first-line with immediate initiation of long-term scheduled high-dose antiepileptic medications
Stage N1 light sleep; managed with urgent stereotactic neurosurgical ablation of hyperactive mesial temporal amygdaloid nuclei
Stage N2 sleep spindles; managed with continuous positive airway pressure mask ventilation and supplemental nocturnal oxygenation
Wake-sleep transition state; managed with high-dose dopamine receptor antagonist medications and daytime psychostimulant therapy

explanation: Sleepwalking (somnambulism) is a Non-REM arousal parasomnia that arises from Stage N3 Slow-Wave Sleep, most commonly occurring during the first third of the night when N3 sleep is most abundant. It involves complex, semi-purposeful motor behaviors (such as sitting up, walking around the house, dressing, or eating) executed during deep sleep. Patients have open eyes with a blank stare, impaired responsiveness, and difficulty being awakened; they exhibit complete morning amnesia. Precipitating factors include sleep deprivation, fever, stress, and obstructive sleep apnea. Primary management is environmental safety (locking doors and windows, removing bedroom obstacles/cords, gate at stairs) and reassurance, as most children outgrow it by adolescence.
high_yield_pearl: Sleepwalking (Somnambulism): Stage N3 Non-REM parasomnia (first 1/3 of night). Blank stare, unarousable, morning amnesia. Management = bedroom safety & sleep hygiene.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 2, 5 & Content Q1: Nocturnal Enuresis
question: A 7-year-old boy has primary nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting at least 3 nights per week without ever achieving 6 continuous months of nighttime dryness). Physical examination and urinalysis are normal. During which sleep stage does enuresis most commonly occur, and what is the most effective first-line behavioral and pharmacologic treatment strategy?

options.text: Stage N3 Non-REM slow-wave sleep; managed first-line with an enuresis moisture alarm, followed by oral desmopressin if needed
Stage N1 light sleep; managed first-line with central nervous system psychostimulants like oral methylphenidate taken at bedtime
Stage REM sleep; managed first-line with continuous positive airway pressure mask ventilation and supplemental nighttime oxygen
Awake quiet rest; managed first-line with high-dose loop diuretics like oral furosemide administered immediately before sleep
Stage N2 sleep spindles; managed first-line with bilateral sacral nerve root surgical rhizotomy to denervate the detrusor muscle

explanation: Nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting) is involuntary urination during sleep in a child $\ge$5 years of age. It most frequently occurs during Stage N3 Non-REM slow-wave sleep (and N2), reflecting a mismatch between nocturnal urine production, bladder functional capacity, and central arousal mechanisms (the child fails to wake up to bladder stretch signals). Management: 1) First-line behavioral therapy: motivational therapy and an enuresis moisture alarm (the most effective long-term therapy with the lowest relapse rate; conditions the child to wake to bladder fullness). 2) First-line pharmacotherapy (for rapid, short-term relief, e.g., for camp or sleepovers): Desmopressin (DDAVP, a synthetic V2 vasopressin agonist that increases water reabsorption in renal collecting ducts, reducing nocturnal urine volume).
high_yield_pearl: Nocturnal Enuresis: Stage N3 Non-REM sleep. First-line behavioral = Enuresis alarm. First-line medication = Desmopressin (DDAVP, V2 agonist).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 4: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)
question: A 52-year-old obese man (BMI 36 kg/m2, neck circumference 18.5 inches) presents with severe daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and dry mouth. His wife reports that he snores loudly and periodically stops breathing during sleep for 20 to 30 seconds, followed by a loud, gasping snort that wakes her up. Laboratory testing reveals polycythemia (hematocrit 56%) and systemic hypertension (155/95 mmHg). What is the fundamental anatomical and physiological mechanism of this disorder?

options.text: Transient cessation of central medullary rhythmic respiratory drive resulting from bilateral phrenic motor neuron demyelination and axonal atrophy
Severe episodic bronchospasm and dynamic expiratory small airway collapse mediated by massive inflammatory leukotriene hypersecretion in lung airways
Chronic restrictive alveolar hypoventilation caused by severe advanced ankylosing spondylitis fusion across all thoracic costovertebral facet joints
Autoimmune antibody destruction targeting carotid body peripheral oxygen chemoreceptor glomus cells, abolishing central hypoxic ventilatory drives
Repetitive collapse and occlusion of the upper pharyngeal airway during sleep due to loss of dilator muscle tone against negative inspiratory pressure

explanation: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is characterized by repetitive episodes of partial (hypopnea) or complete (apnea) collapse of the upper pharyngeal airway during sleep. Factors predisposing to collapse include excess pharyngeal adipose tissue (obesity, thick neck), craniofacial retrognathia, enlarged tonsils, and the physiological relaxation of pharyngeal dilator muscles (particularly the genioglossus, innervated by CN XII) during sleep onset. Inspiratory negative intrathoracic pressure sucks the floppy airway walls shut, causing airflow cessation despite persistent, vigorous thoracic and abdominal respiratory efforts. The resulting nocturnal hypoxemia and hypercapnia trigger autonomic sympathetic surges (causing hypertension) and stimulate renal erythropoietin secretion (causing secondary polycythemia).
high_yield_pearl: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA): Pharyngeal airway collapse despite persistent respiratory effort $\rightarrow$ hypoxia, micro-arousals, daytime somnolence, hypertension, polycythemia.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 4: OSA Polysomnography & CPAP
question: A patient with loud snoring, daytime hypersomnolence, and witnessed apneas undergoes an overnight polysomnogram. The study calculates the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI). Which threshold confirms the diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea, and what is the gold-standard, first-line therapy that pneumatically splints the pharynx open?

options.text: An AHI of $\ge$ 5 events per hour with symptoms (or $\ge$ 15 without); treated first-line with Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP)
An AHI of $\ge$ 1 event per hour regardless of daytime manifestations; treated first-line with emergency bilateral permanent tracheostomy
An AHI of $\ge$ 100 events per hour during Stage REM sleep; treated first-line with high-dose respiratory stimulants such as oral theophylline
An AHI of $\ge$ 50 events per hour on polysomnography; treated first-line with radical surgical uvulopalatopharyngoplasty in all adult patients
An AHI of $\ge$ 30 events per hour with severe arterial desaturation; treated first-line with nocturnal low-flow supplemental nasal oxygen alone

explanation: The diagnosis of OSA is confirmed by overnight polysomnography demonstrating an elevated Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI, the average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep). Diagnostic criteria: AHI $\ge$ 5 events/hr in the presence of symptoms (daytime somnolence, fatigue, snoring, witnessed apneas, hypertension), or AHI $\ge$ 15 events/hr regardless of symptoms. (Severity: mild 5-14, moderate 15-29, severe $\ge$30). The gold-standard first-line treatment is Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP). CPAP delivers a continuous column of pressurized room air via a nasal or full-face mask, acting as a 'pneumatic stent' that prevents the soft palate, tongue, and lateral pharyngeal walls from collapsing during inspiration.
high_yield_pearl: OSA diagnosis: AHI $\ge$ 5/hr with symptoms (or $\ge$ 15/hr). Gold standard treatment = Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4: Central Sleep Apnea & Cheyne-Stokes
question: A 72-year-old man with severe ischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 22%) undergoes polysomnography for daytime fatigue. The study demonstrates cyclical episodes characterized by a gradual crescendo-decrescendo pattern of tidal breathing separated by 25-second periods of complete airflow cessation during which there is NO thoracic or abdominal respiratory effort. What type of sleep-disordered breathing does this patient have, and what mechanism drives it?

options.text: Sleep-related hypoventilation syndrome caused by progressive bilateral diaphragmatic paralysis secondary to motor neuron anterior horn degeneration
Central sleep apnea with Cheyne-Stokes breathing, driven by delayed circulatory time and heightened chemoreceptor sensitivity to carbon dioxide
Obstructive sleep apnea with pharyngeal airway soft tissue collapse occurring despite persistent, vigorous thoracoabdominal diaphragmatic efforts
Severe inspiratory stridor caused by bilateral vocal cord adductor paralysis secondary to surgical recurrent laryngeal nerve traumatic transections
Catathrenia characterized by prolonged, monotonic expiratory vocal cord groaning accompanied by bradypnea during deep Stage REM sleep cycles

explanation: Central Sleep Apnea (CSA) is characterized by temporary cessation of respiratory effort due to loss of central ventilatory drive from the medullary respiratory centers (unlike OSA, there is NO respiratory effort during the apnea). Cheyne-Stokes respiration is a unique form of CSA classically seen in severe congestive heart failure (and stroke): prolonged circulation time (due to low cardiac output) delays the transport of arterial blood gases from the lungs to the central chemoreceptors. When PaCO2 rises, hyper-responsive chemoreceptors trigger severe hyperventilation (crescendo); this drives PaCO2 below the 'apneic threshold', causing central cessation of all respiratory drive (apnea, decrescendo) until PaCO2 re-accumulates, repeating the cycle.
high_yield_pearl: Central Sleep Apnea / Cheyne-Stokes: NO respiratory effort during apnea. Crescendo-decrescendo breathing in heart failure (delayed circulation time + chemoreceptor overshooting).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome
question: A 56-year-old man with extreme obesity (BMI 44 kg/m2) is evaluated for chronic dyspnea, somnolence, and ankle edema. An arterial blood gas drawn while breathing room air at rest during the DAY demonstrates: pH 7.36, PaO2 58 mmHg, PaCO2 52 mmHg, and serum bicarbonate 31 mEq/L. Polysomnography demonstrates frequent obstructive events. What condition is defined by this awake daytime hypercapnia in an obese patient, and how does the body compensate?

options.text: Idiopathic central sleep apnea; total suppression of renal renin-angiotensin-aldosterone signaling
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (Pickwickian syndrome); renal retention of bicarbonate buffers chronic respiratory acidosis
Metabolic ketoacidosis; respiratory hyperventilation through rapid Kussmaul respirations
Primary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis; severe metabolic lactic acidosis with anion gap elevation
Pure uncomplicated obstructive sleep apnea; acute respiratory alkalosis with urinary potassium excretion

explanation: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS, historically called Pickwickian syndrome) is clinically defined by the triad of: 1) Obesity (BMI $\ge$ 30 kg/m2), 2) Daytime awake alveolar hypoventilation resulting in hypercapnia (PaCO2 > 45 mmHg), and 3) Hypoxemia (PaO2 < 70 mmHg), in the absence of other primary causes of hypoventilation (such as severe COPD or neuromuscular disease). Approximately 90% of patients with OHS have co-existing severe OSA. The massive chest wall and abdominal mass load increase the work of breathing; blunted central respiratory drive fails to compensate. The kidneys compensate for chronic respiratory acidosis by retaining bicarbonate (elevated HCO3- >27 mEq/L).
high_yield_pearl: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (Pickwickian): BMI $\ge$ 30 + Awake DAYTIME hypercapnia (PaCO2 > 45 mmHg) + Hypoxemia. Renal retention of HCO3- buffers acidosis.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 5: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS)
question: A 38-year-old woman presents with distressing sensations in both of her lower legs. She describes an uncomfortable 'creeping, crawling, and pulling' feeling deep within her calves that occurs exclusively when she is resting or lying in bed in the evening. She feels an overwhelming, irresistible urge to move her legs, and pacing around the bedroom or shaking her legs temporarily relieves the discomfort. What is the diagnosis, and which laboratory parameter must be screened?

options.text: Restless legs syndrome (Willis-Ekbom disease); serum ferritin must be measured to evaluate for iron deficiency
Deep vein thrombosis of the lower extremity; plasma D-dimer and venous duplex ultrasound must be performed
Acute compartment syndrome; intracompartmental needle pressure must be measured urgently
Intermittent neurogenic claudication; lumbar spine MRI must be obtained to assess spinal stenosis
Peripheral diabetic polyneuropathy; fasting blood glucose and hemoglobin A1c must be checked

explanation: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS, Willis-Ekbom disease) is a common sensorimotor disorder characterized by four essential diagnostic criteria: 1) An irresistible urge to move the legs, usually accompanied by uncomfortable paresthesias/dysesthesias deep in the limbs. 2) Symptoms begin or worsen during periods of rest or inactivity (sitting or lying down). 3) Symptoms are partially or totally relieved by movement (walking, stretching, rubbing) for as long as the movement continues. 4) Symptoms are worse or occur exclusively in the evening or at night (circadian pattern). Pathophysiology involves central dopaminergic dysfunction and central iron deficiency in the substantia nigra. All patients must have their serum ferritin checked; iron deficiency (ferritin <50-75 ng/mL) is a key reversible trigger.
high_yield_pearl: Restless Legs Syndrome: Urge to move legs at rest in evening, relieved by movement. Linked to CNS iron deficiency; check serum ferritin (supplement if <50-75 ng/mL).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Case 5: Restless Legs Syndrome Pharmacology
question: A 45-year-old man with restless legs syndrome whose serum ferritin is normal (110 ng/mL) continues to experience severe nightly symptoms that prevent him from falling asleep. What are the two primary first-line classes of pharmacotherapy used for restless legs syndrome, and what major complication can occur with chronic dopamine agonist use?

options.text: First-generation sedating antihistamines or tricyclic antidepressants; both classes carry a high clinical risk of precipitating lethal serotonin syndromes
Long-acting barbiturate hypnotics or direct skeletal muscle relaxants; both drug classes carry prominent warnings for acute fulminant toxic hepatic necrosis
High-ceiling loop diuretics or dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers; both classes carry high risks of precipitating irreversible sensorineural ototoxicity
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or peripheral beta-blockers; both classes carry a substantial risk of triggering severe neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Alpha-2-delta calcium channel ligands (gabapentin/pregabalin) or dopamine agonists (pramipexole/ropinirole); dopamine agonists carry the risk of augmentation

explanation: First-line pharmacotherapy for Restless Legs Syndrome includes: 1) Alpha-2-delta calcium channel ligands: Gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin, or pregabalin (bind to $\alpha_2\delta$ subunits of voltage-gated calcium channels to decrease presynaptic glutamate release; currently preferred as initial therapy due to lack of augmentation risk). 2) Non-ergot dopamine receptor agonists: Pramipexole, ropinirole, or rotigotine (D2/D3 agonists). Critical clinical complication of chronic dopamine agonist therapy: Augmentation, a phenomenon where RLS symptoms become progressively more severe, occur earlier in the afternoon or morning, spread to the upper extremities, and occur after shorter periods of rest. If augmentation develops, the dopamine agonist must be tapered and switched to an alpha-2-delta ligand.
high_yield_pearl: RLS pharmacotherapy: First-line = Alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin/pregabalin) or Dopamine agonists (pramipexole/ropinirole). Dopamine agonist risk = Augmentation.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4: Delayed Sleep Phase Syndrome (DSPD)
question: A 17-year-old high school senior is brought to clinic by his parents because he cannot fall asleep before 3:00 AM on school nights. Every morning when his alarm sounds at 6:30 AM, he is combative and nearly impossible to wake up, leading to chronic truancy and falling grades. However, on weekends and summer vacations when allowed to sleep on his own schedule, he sleeps soundly from 3:30 AM to 11:30 AM (8 continuous hours) and awakens refreshed. What is the diagnosis, and what is the optimal management?

options.text: Delayed sleep phase disorder (DSPD); managed with morning bright light therapy and low-dose evening melatonin
Chronic primary psychophysiological insomnia; managed with strict sleep restriction therapy
Advanced sleep phase disorder; managed with evening bright light and morning darkness
Major depressive disorder with terminal insomnia; managed with bedtime tricyclic antidepressants
Narcolepsy Type 1; managed with lifelong high-dose modafinil and sodium oxybate

explanation: Delayed Sleep Phase Disorder (DSPD) is a circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder characterized by a stable, intractable delay in the timing of the major sleep period relative to standard societal and environmental norms (typically delayed by $\ge$2 hours). It is highly prevalent in adolescents and young adults (~7-16%). When free from social constraints (weekends/holidays), sleep architecture and total sleep duration are completely normal, but shifted forward in time (e.g., sleeping 3 AM to 11 AM). Clinical conflict arises when early school or work schedules force early awakening, resulting in severe chronic sleep deprivation. Management: chronotherapy, timed bright light exposure immediately upon morning awakening (to advance the circadian phase), and low-dose exogenous melatonin (0.5-3 mg) administered 4 to 5 hours prior to the desired bedtime.
high_yield_pearl: Delayed Sleep Phase Disorder ('extreme night owls', teens): Sleep architecture normal but shifted late (3 AM - 11 AM). Treat: Morning bright light + evening melatonin.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4: Advanced Sleep Phase Syndrome (ASPS)
question: A 74-year-old retired accountant presents with a complaint of falling asleep between 6:30 PM and 7:00 PM every evening while watching the early news. He awakens completely alert and unable to return to sleep between 2:30 AM and 3:00 AM every morning. Several members of his family across three generations exhibited identical early sleep habits. Which genetic mutation in the core molecular circadian feedback loop has been linked to familial Advanced Sleep Phase Syndrome (ASPS)?

options.text: X-linked recessive mutations in the hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT) gene
Trinucleotide CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene on chromosome 4
Contiguous microdeletion of the elastin gene on chromosome 7q11.23
Autosomal recessive mutations in the survival motor neuron 1 (SMN1) gene
Autosomal dominant mutations in the PER2 (period 2) or CK1D (casein kinase 1 delta) circadian clock genes

explanation: Advanced Sleep Phase Disorder (ASPD) is a circadian rhythm disorder characterized by a persistent, involuntary shift of the sleep-wake schedule to an earlier time: patients experience overwhelming sleepiness in the early evening (6 to 8 PM) and awaken early in the morning (2 to 4 AM). While common as an acquired age-related change in the elderly, an inherited form (Familial Advanced Sleep Phase Syndrome, FASPS) follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Molecular genetic studies have linked FASPS to missense mutations in core circadian clock genes: PER2 (period circadian regulator 2) or CK1D (casein kinase 1 delta), which accelerates phosphorylation and nuclear clearance of clock proteins, shortening the intrinsic circadian period. Management includes evening bright light exposure (to delay the circadian phase).
high_yield_pearl: Advanced Sleep Phase Disorder ('early birds', elderly/familial): Early evening sleepiness (7 PM) + early morning awakening (3 AM). Familial FASPS linked to PER2/CK1D mutations.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4: Jet Lag & Travel Direction
question: A business executive flies from New York to London (traveling EASTWARD across 5 time zones) for a conference, and flies from London to New York (traveling WESTWARD) two weeks later. She notes that her jet lag symptoms (insomnia, fatigue, gastrointestinal distress) are substantially more severe and take twice as many days to resolve following the eastward flight. Why is eastward travel biologically more difficult to adapt to than westward travel?

options.text: Eastward transmeridian flight completely and permanently abolishes enzymatic serotonin N-acetyltransferase synthesis of melatonin within the pineal gland
Atmospheric commercial aircraft cabin pressurization drops substantially below physiological baselines when flying transatlantically across oceanic zones
The anterior suprachiasmatic nucleus master pacemaker intrinsically lacks efferent neural projections capable of accelerating clock gene transcription rates
Eastward flight navigation vectors travel directly against the Earth's natural Coriolis gravitational rotational vector and geomagnetic polar fields
Eastward travel requires advancing (shortening) the circadian cycle, which is harder because the human endogenous circadian period naturally exceeds 24 hours

explanation: Jet Lag Disorder occurs when rapid transmeridian travel across multiple time zones produces a temporary desynchronization between the internal circadian clock and local environmental light-dark cues. Traveling EASTWARD (which requires PHASE ADVANCE: going to bed earlier and waking earlier) is universally more difficult to adapt to than traveling WESTWARD (which requires PHASE DELAY: going to bed later and waking later). This occurs because the intrinsic, endogenous human circadian pacemaker (in the SCN) runs on a natural period that is slightly LONGER than 24 hours (~24.2 to 24.5 hours in most humans). Therefore, the biological clock naturally drifts toward lengthening/delaying the day (westward), whereas forcing the clock to shorten/advance (eastward) requires strenuous daily phase-resetting (~1 day per time zone traveled east vs. 0.5-0.7 days west).
high_yield_pearl: Jet lag: Traveling EAST (phase advance / going to sleep earlier) is much harder than traveling WEST (phase delay) because intrinsic human circadian rhythm is >24 hours.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4 & Content Q4: Chronic Insomnia & CBT-I
question: A 42-year-old corporate attorney reports difficulty falling asleep (taking >60 minutes) and frequent nighttime awakenings occurring 5 nights per week for the past 6 months. She spends 10 hours in bed tossing and turning, checking the clock, answering work emails on her smartphone, and worrying about tomorrow's fatigue. Physical exam and laboratory tests are normal. What is the gold-standard, first-line treatment for chronic primary insomnia?

options.text: High-dose oral over-the-counter diphenhydramine taken nightly for one year
Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) titration regardless of sleep study results
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I), incorporating stimulus control and sleep restriction
Immediate surgical resection of the pineal gland to eliminate nighttime melatonin
Indefinite long-term prescription of high-dose oral alprazolam at bedtime

explanation: Chronic Insomnia is defined by difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or early morning awakening, occurring at least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months, despite adequate opportunity for sleep, accompanied by daytime impairment (fatigue, poor concentration, mood disturbance). The gold-standard, first-line therapy recommended by all major medical guidelines is Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I). CBT-I is superior to pharmacotherapy in long-term efficacy and lacks side effects. Key components: 1) Stimulus control: go to bed only when sleepy; use bed only for sleep and sex; leave the bedroom if awake after 20 minutes. 2) Sleep restriction: limit time in bed to match actual sleep time, consolidating sleep. 3) Sleep hygiene: regular sleep schedule, no screens/caffeine/alcohol before bed. 4) Cognitive restructuring.
high_yield_pearl: Chronic Insomnia: First-line gold standard = Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I: stimulus control, sleep restriction, sleep hygiene).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4: Dual Orexin Receptor Antagonists (DORAs)
question: A 50-year-old woman with chronic sleep-onset and sleep-maintenance insomnia is prescribed suvorexant. By which pharmacologic mechanism does this medication promote sleep, and what advantage does it have over traditional benzodiazepine receptor agonists?

options.text: Binds to GABA-A receptor alpha-1 subunits to open chloride ion channels, causing significant motor incoordination and severe morning anterograde amnesia
Stimulates central histamine H1 receptors in the tuberomammillary nucleus of the posterior hypothalamus to paradoxically induce deep cortical sedation
Blocks orexin OX1 and OX2 receptors to inhibit wakefulness pathways, without causing GABAergic physical dependence or disrupting sleep architecture
Activates MT1 and MT2 G-protein coupled melatonin receptors situated within the anterior hypothalamic suprachiasmatic master circadian pacemaker nucleus
Inhibits presynaptic serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake transporters located within synapses across frontocortical and monoaminergic brainstem networks

explanation: Dual Orexin Receptor Antagonists (DORAs, e.g., suvorexant, lemborexant, daridorexant) represent a modern class of insomnia medications. Rather than acting as general central nervous system depressants (like GABA-A agonists), DORAs have a targeted mechanism: they act as competitive antagonists at both the Orexin-1 (OX1R) and Orexin-2 (OX2R) receptors in the brain. By blocking the binding of wake-promoting neuropeptides orexin-A and orexin-B, DORAs turn down the active wakefulness drive, allowing the natural sleep switch (VLPO) to take over. Advantages: they do not cause respiratory depression, have minimal risk of physical dependence or withdrawal, and preserve physiological sleep architecture (Stages N3 and REM).
high_yield_pearl: Dual Orexin Receptor Antagonists (Suvorexant, Lemborexant): Block OX1 and OX2 receptors $\rightarrow$ turn off wake drive. No GABAergic dependence.

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4: Non-Benzodiazepine Hypnotics (Z-Drugs)
question: A 36-year-old woman with acute sleep-onset insomnia is prescribed zolpidem for short-term use. By which molecular mechanism do the 'Z-drugs' (zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone) facilitate sleep, and which adverse behavioral phenomenon is a recognized boxed warning for this drug class?

options.text: Blockade of voltage-gated L-type calcium channels in the heart; carries a risk of complete AV block
Irreversible inhibition of monoamine oxidase A and B; carries a risk of hypertensive tyramine crisis
Direct stimulation of dopamine D2 receptors in the striatum; carries a risk of severe acute dystonic reactions
Selective agonism at the alpha-1 subunit of the GABA-A receptor; carries a risk of complex sleep behaviors like sleep-driving and sleep-eating
Competitive antagonism of central muscarinic M1 receptors; carries a risk of acute angle-closure glaucoma

explanation: The non-benzodiazepine hypnotics ('Z-drugs': zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone) act as selective positive allosteric modulators at the alpha-1 ($\alpha_1$) subunit of the ionotropic GABA-A receptor complex. The $\alpha_1$ subunit mediates sedation and sleep, whereas $\alpha_2$ and $\alpha_3$ subunits mediate anxiolysis and muscle relaxation. Because of this $\alpha_1$ selectivity, Z-drugs produce rapid sedation with less anticonvulsant, muscle relaxant, or anxiolytic activity and minimal disruption of normal slow-wave and REM sleep architecture compared to classic benzodiazepines. However, all Z-drugs carry a black-box warning for complex sleep behaviors (sleepwalking, sleep-driving, sleep-cooking, or sleep-eating while not fully awake, with complete amnesia for the event).
high_yield_pearl: Z-drugs (Zolpidem, Zaleplon, Eszopiclone): Selective GABA-A $\alpha_1$ subunit agonists $\rightarrow$ sedation. Black-box warning for complex sleep behaviors (sleep-driving).

source: Lecture File 17 Slide 4: Fatal Familial Insomnia (FFI)
question: A 48-year-old man of Italian ancestry presents with progressive, relentless insomnia over the past 4 months. He is now completely unable to sleep despite profound exhaustion. He exhibits severe autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, and hypertension), ataxia, tremors, spontaneous myoclonus, and progressive cognitive decline. Genetic analysis confirms an autosomal dominant mutation in the PRNP gene (D178N mutation paired with methionine at codon 129). Autopsy demonstrates selective, profound neuronal loss and astrogliosis restricted to which central brain structure?

options.text: Hippocampal CA1 pyramidal sector and entorhinal cortex
Caudate nucleus and putamen of the dorsal striatum
Substantia nigra pars compacta and locus coeruleus
Ventral anterior and mediodorsal thalamic nuclei
Cerebellar flocculonodular lobe and dentate nucleus

explanation: Fatal Familial Insomnia (FFI) is an extremely rare, fatal, autosomal dominant prion disease caused by a specific missense mutation at codon 178 of the PRNP gene (aspartic acid replaced by asparagine, D178N) coupled with a methionine polymorphism at codon 129 of the same allele. Prion conversion ($PrP^C \rightarrow PrP^{Sc}$) leads to selective, severe neuronal apoptosis and astrogliosis restricted to the thalamus, specifically the mediodorsal and ventral anterior thalamic nuclei. The thalamus serves as a critical gating hub for sleep spindle generation and slow-wave sleep; its destruction causes total, intractable loss of sleep architecture, progressive autonomic instability (sympathetic storm), motor dysfunction (myoclonus, ataxia), and death typically within 7 to 18 months.
high_yield_pearl: Fatal Familial Insomnia (FFI): Autosomal dominant prion disease (PRNP D178N-129M mutation) $\rightarrow$ selective degeneration of THALAMUS (mediodorsal/ventral anterior) $\rightarrow$ total insomnia & death.
